changes.title: Cloudflare Sandbox: an agent harness, faster starts and smaller custom sizes
changes.what: Cloudflare now documents an experimental Agents SDK harness that runs Claude Code or Codex in a container with no Dockerfile, a 648 ms median start on its new runtime, an interactive terminal through exec(), and custom sizes from 1/16 of a vCPU. Account concurrency rose tenfold to 15,000 vCPU. Its limits page dropped the 3 GiB-per-vCPU memory rule that a September changelog still states; this guide keeps pricing the standard presets, so the A/B/C costs are unchanged. It also adds a 24 September disclosure that a shared storage pool let customers recover each other’s leftover disk blocks, fixed by 19 September. The date is when this guide checked, not when Cloudflare made each change.

sources.quote: No Dockerfile is needed.
| Concurrent vCPU | 15,000 |
a customer with a Workers Paid account could recover residual disk blocks previously used by Containers on the same host.

changes.title: E2B: private sandbox URLs by default, agent templates and a lower Enterprise floor
changes.what: Projects created since 30 October 2026 put sandbox URLs behind a per-sandbox traffic token, and E2B now ships ready-made templates for Claude Code, Codex, Amp, OpenClaw and six other agents. A fifth region, US East on AWS, can be enabled through support. The free Hobby plan now allows 10 concurrent sandboxes instead of 20, and Enterprise starts at a $2,000 monthly commit instead of a $3,000 minimum. Per-second rates did not change, so the A/B/C costs stand. The date is when this guide checked, not when E2B made each change.

sources.quote: **New projects:** since October 30, 2026, newly created projects default to private sandbox traffic.
Up to 10 concurrently running sandboxes.
Enterprise starts at a $2,000/mo commit, 500 concurrent included.

changes.title: Tensorlake now bills at least 20% of allocated CPU
changes.what: Tensorlake's pricing page now bills CPU at a minimum of 20% of the vCPU you allocate, so a mostly idle sandbox costs more: workload C rises from $8.26 to $9.52. It also publishes a reserved NVIDIA H100 at $3.95 per GPU-hour, says egress is free, and reported a 7 November security incident in which customer email addresses were read. The date is when this guide checked, not when Tensorlake made each change.

sources.quote: CPU is billed on active execution, with a minimum of 20% of allocated vCPU.
Based on what we know, customer email information was accessed.

changes.title: InstaBox recheck: GPUs, a hosted MCP server and included disk
changes.what: A full recheck found NVIDIA L4 GPU machines at $0.80 per GPU-hour on paid plans, a Python SDK, a hosted MCP server, Docker and OCI image import, copy-on-write forks, a public status page and a SOC 2 Type II report on request. Paid plans now include 200 GiB to 5 TiB of disk, so the always-on workload drops from $27.23 to $24.82 a month. Free runs are capped at 480 minutes. The date is when this guide checked, not when InstaBox launched each change.

sources.quote: NVIDIA L4 (`l4`) | \$0.80 per GPU-hour | 11 vCPU / 36 GiB
Paid plans include disk across all their machines (200 GiB on Pro, 1 TiB on Builder, 5 TiB on Team)
The hosted server at `https://api.instabox.sh/mcp` is the recommended way to connect.

changes.title: TierHive added: near-free hourly servers that are still in Alpha
changes.what: This guide now lists TierHive, a build-your-own NAT server billed by the hour with a one-hour minimum per server and at most 2 vCPU. Its own policy says it is in Alpha, that data loss can happen without warning and that there is no uptime promise, so it carries no recommendations here. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: Data loss can occur at any time without warning
We do not guarantee any specific uptime or Service Level Agreement (SLA)

changes.title: HostHatch added: fixed monthly servers on its own hardware, with no SLA
changes.what: This guide now lists HostHatch, sold in fixed monthly plans from $4. A stopped server still bills for the month, and its terms have no uptime promise. Prices here are the published monthly list prices; the checkout prices for longer terms are behind a login. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: Our smallest plan costs $4 per month

changes.title: Correction: Tensorlake does promise 99.9% uptime on paid plans
changes.what: This guide's capability checklist said Tensorlake had no uptime promise. Its Terms promise 99.9% monthly availability for the control plane on paid plans, with service credits applied automatically. The Terms also set a 4-hour first response for critical tickets, while the pricing page says 24 hours on Pro. The date is when this guide corrected it, not a change by Tensorlake.

sources.quote: TensorLake will use commercially reasonable efforts to make the Control Plane available 99.9% of the time in each calendar month
This Section 5 applies to paid Plans and does not apply to Free Offerings (Section 12).
applies them automatically to Customer’s next invoice; Customer is not required to submit a claim

changes.title: Scaleway added: French hourly servers whose compute stops billing when off
changes.what: This guide now lists Scaleway Instances, priced in euros and shown in US dollars at the ECB rate. Each resource bills by the hour with a 60-minute minimum. Powering off stops the compute meter, but the block volume and a flexible IPv4 keep billing. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: Each of these resources is billed separately for a minimum of 60 minutes.

changes.title: Contabo added: low monthly VPS prices, with a reputation to weigh
changes.what: This guide now lists Contabo. Its headline price is the 24-month rate; month-to-month Cloud VPS 4 is $6.60. CPU cores are shared, there is no hourly meter and a stopped server still bills. See the What users say section before buying. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: The price displayed is the effective monthly rate for a 24-month subscription including applicable taxes

changes.title: Vultr added: hourly VMs in 34 regions, capped at the monthly price
changes.what: This guide now lists Vultr. Servers bill by the hour with a one-hour minimum, up to a monthly cap, and keep billing while stopped. Vultr's own pages give three different hourly rates for the same plan; the guide uses the monthly price divided by 672, as its billing FAQ describes. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: The minimum billing unit is one hour, and hourly charges begin when a server is deployed, regardless of whether it is powered on or off.

changes.title: Akamai Cloud (Linode) added: hourly VMs with one-click Hermes and OpenClaw
changes.what: This guide now lists Akamai Cloud, still called Linode in its plans, API and console. Machines bill by the hour, rounded up, up to a monthly cap, and keep billing while powered off. Hermes Agent and OpenClaw have Quick Deploy apps. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: Most paid services offered on Akamai Cloud have predictable monthly rates, also called the monthly caps, alongside flexible hourly rates.

changes.title: Amazon Lightsail added: fixed-price AWS servers billed by the hour
changes.what: This guide now lists Amazon Lightsail, AWS's bundle-priced virtual servers. Bundles run from $5 to $1,764 a month, are billed per hour up to that cap, and keep billing while stopped. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: Bundles are billed on an on-demand hourly rate, so you pay only for what you use.

changes.title: OVHcloud added: monthly VPS plans with n8n preinstalled
changes.what: This guide now lists OVHcloud's VPS range, priced from the US order catalog in USD before tax on the no-commitment monthly term. A switched-off VPS still bills. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: You can choose to be billed monthly for a Virtual Private Server (VPS) regardless of whether you select a commitment that is month-to-month, 12 months, or 24 months.

changes.title: Freestyle added: full Linux VMs that pause with memory and fork live
changes.what: This guide now lists Freestyle. Its VMs bill per second on allocated vCPU, memory and storage, with monthly allowances on every plan; Hobby is a $50 monthly minimum usable as usage. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: | **Hobby** | $50/month minimum, including $50 usage | Up to 40 |

changes.title: HostUp added: a Swedish VPS with seven fixed monthly plans
changes.what: This guide now lists HostUp, a VPS provider with one data hall in Stockholm. Plans are billed by the month whether the server runs or is stopped; prices here are HostUp's own USD display, before VAT. The date is when this guide checked it, not a launch date.

sources.quote: If you are a private customer in an EU country, you can choose whether prices in the client area include VAT.

changes.title: Lizard added two bigger plans, Pro 5x and Pro 20x
changes.what: Lizard's pricing page now lists Pro 5x at $99 a month and Pro 20x at $499, alongside Pro at $19. Each includes its fee back as usage and raises the sandbox limits; neither has a trial. Sandbox rates per size did not change, so no cost figure on this site moves.

sources.quote: Pro 5x is $99 a month with $99 of usage included. Beyond that, pay as you go. It has no trial.

changes.title: Sprites' rates are roughly half the figures still in circulation
changes.what: Fly's current list is $0.0385 per CPU-hour and $0.021875 per GB-hour, both measured on actual use. A widely copied comparison still narrates $0.07 and $0.04375. Fly publishes no change date, so this entry is dated by observation, not by an announcement. The same pricing page says there are no plans, while the Sprites FAQ describes a plan ladder that includes Hero at $100 a month and goes up to Mythic at $2,000.

changes.title: boxd cut its rates by about a fifth and doubled the machine quota in 19 days
changes.what: The 9 October capture of boxd's pricing page lists €0.049 per vCPU-hour, €0.015 per GiB-hour of RAM, €0.0001 per GiB-hour of disk and 50 machines. The live page lists €0.039, €0.012, €0.00008 and 100 machines. boxd publishes no price-change notice, and its terms let it adjust rates at any time for usage from the date of the change.

sources.quote: €0.049 / vCPU-hour
100 machines included, raiseable on request

changes.title: InstaBox put a price on a product that was two weeks old
changes.what: InstaBox launched on 14 October 2026 and published pricing five days later: $20, $100 and $500 plans that double as credit, plus a free plan with one 4 vCPU / 8 GiB machine. It is the second product from InsForge AI, whose first product is a backend platform.

sources.quote: Today we're releasing InstaBox pricing.

changes.title: Runtime changed its idle pause from one minute to five
changes.what: A sandbox now pauses after 300 seconds with no request, command, connection, traffic or CPU use, where the default was 60 seconds. The changelog is the only announcement; the pricing page carries the current number.

sources.quote: Idle sandboxes now pause after 5 minutes.

changes.title: Lizard's sandboxes became Firecracker microVMs, and the meter became a flat price per size
changes.what: On 30 September 2026 Lizard's own limits page said sandboxes ran in Kubernetes pods on a shared kernel at a fixed 4 vCPU / 4096 MiB, billed on measured CPU, memory, storage and egress. By 13 October the pricing page listed three sizes at a flat hourly rate. Neither page announced the change and there is no migration note. The billing model changed; no published figure shows that any bill went up.

sources.quote: Sandboxes run short-lived commands and agent tasks in Kubernetes pods with the runc runtime. They share the host kernel; they are not Firecracker virtual machines.
Small 2 vCPU · 4 GB RAM · 5 GB disk

changes.title: InstaBox launched as a second product from InsForge
changes.what: The sandbox product went public on 14 October 2026, about a year after the company was founded and seven months after its Y Combinator batch. The YC badge sits on insforge.dev, not on instabox.sh.

sources.quote: Since we launched on Oct 14, beta users have been using InstaBox for free.

changes.title: Tensorlake's npm SDK release 0.5.144 was malicious for about 100 minutes
changes.what: A compromised maintainer account published a credential-stealing version of the JavaScript SDK through Tensorlake's own release workflow. Only the npm package was affected; 0.5.143 and earlier are safe. The date is the one in Tensorlake's advisory.

sources.quote: The package was live on npm for approximately 1 hour 40 minutes (01:12–02:54 UTC). Only the npm package was affected, the PyPI and crates.io `tensorlake` packages and the `tensorlake` CLI were not.

changes.title: OVHcloud rebooted about a million VMs to patch a KVM flaw
changes.what: OVHcloud patched the CVE-2026-53359 KVM vulnerability across tens of thousands of hosts, starting with VPS hosts on 8 July, and its own write-up records corrupted data on several VMs in 3 clusters. The date is the start of patching in OVHcloud's post.

sources.quote: environ un million de machines virtuelles
données corrompues sur plusieurs VMs réparties sur 3 clusters

changes.title: Box became Boat
changes.what: The product launched as box in July 2026 and was renamed boat on 15 September 2026. Box endpoints still answer, with Deprecation and Sunset headers; the Sunset date is a warning, not a shutdown. The legal entity, Dedale AI, Corp., did not change.

sources.quote: Box became **boat** on September 15, 2026.

changes.title: Baseten acquired Blaxel
changes.what: Baseten announced the acquisition on 10 September 2026 and said the product continues unchanged, with new Baseten products to follow. Each Baseten organisation now maps to one Blaxel workspace. The standard terms linked from Blaxel's site are dated 10 December 2025 and still name Blaxel, Inc., so the contracting entity after the deal is worth confirming in writing.

sources.quote: Baseten has acquired Blaxel.
Each Baseten organization maps to one dedicated Blaxel workspace and one dedicated Blaxel account.

changes.title: Daytona raised $60M at a $1B valuation
changes.what: Daytona's Series B, led by FirstMark Growth, brings total funding to $91M. It is the same month the company's open-source repository was archived and core development moved to a private codebase.

sources.quote: a $60M Series B at a $1B valuation, led by FirstMark Growth, bringing our total funding to $91M

changes.title: Modal raised $750M and said Sandboxes alone runs at $300M
changes.what: The Series D values Modal at $15.75B post-money and takes total funding over $1.2B. The same post says the company crossed $1B in annualized run rate and that Sandboxes is a $300M run-rate product on its own.

sources.quote: we've raised a $750M Series D at a $15.75B post-money valuation. Accel led the round.

changes.title: Cloudflare Containers and Sandboxes became generally available
changes.what: The GA entry is in the changelog, not a marketing page. Two parts of the product are still in public beta: the Durable Object scheduling policy that sandboxes use, and container snapshots. The 1.0 helper library arrived on 30 September 2026, and the 0.x SDK gets fixes only until 31 December 2026.

sources.quote: Cloudflare Containers and Sandboxes are now generally available.

changes.title: DigitalOcean Droplets moved from hourly to per-second billing
changes.what: DigitalOcean's pricing page says Droplets bill per second from 1 January 2026, with a minimum of 60 seconds or $0.01 per Droplet, whichever is higher. The 672-hour monthly cap stayed, so an always-on Droplet still costs its flat monthly price, and a powered-off Droplet is still billed. The date is the one DigitalOcean gives; this guide recorded it on 29 October 2026.

sources.quote: Effective January 1, 2026, we're moving to per-second billing (with a minimum charge of 60 seconds or $0.01, whichever is higher) for Droplets.
